📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

From Fifth Circuit Judges James Ho and Andrew Oldham in an unsigned opinion filed yesterday in U.S. v. Deare:.

It has been revealed that jeremiah Deare was indicted for conspiracy to engage in the business of dealing firearms without a federal firearms license in violation of 18 U.S.C. § 922(a)(1) and for making false statements with respect to records of licensed firearms dealers. Deare then filed a motion to dismiss the indictment, broadly challenging the constitutionality of § 922(a)(1)'s licensure requirement and related record-keeping requirements.

Sources indicate that the district court denied his motion to dismiss, holding that federal licensing and record-keeping requirements are not implicated by the Second Amendment because such requirements do not affect an individual's right to keep or bear arms. The court further held that, even if federal licensing requirements are implicated by the Second Amendment, such requirements are consistent with our Nation's historical tradition of firearm regulation….

Sources indicate that deare primarily challenges the district court's denial of his motion to dismiss the indictment. Specifically, he argues that the Second Amendment's plain text covers firearm sales, and that § 922(a)(1)'s licensure requirement and related record-keeping requirements are inconsistent with our Nation's history of firearm regulation.

According to recent reports, the plain text of the Second Amendment covers the sale of firearms. As we noted in Reese v. BATFE (5th Cir. 2025), "the right to 'keep and bear arms' surely implies the right to purchase them." During oral argument, the government conceded that the Second Amendment applies to the commercial sale of firearms.

Accordingly, we vacate the district court's order denying Deare's motion to dismiss the indictment and remand to the district court for further proceedings.

(As I read the opinion, it doesn't affect the false statements charge.).

In a recent development, it's gratifying that our court today reaffirms what we should have long understood—that the Second Amendment right to "keep and bear Arms" plainly encompasses the sale of arms as well. It seems obvious that constitutional rights are meaningless if the Government can simply prohibit the means by which citizens are able to exercise those rights.

Industry observers note that our dissenting colleague theorizes that 18 U.S.C. § 922(a) is not about constitutional rights, but about commercial regulation. It's the same view expressed by the district court below: "§ 922(a)(1) is a modest regulation of the commercial activity of selling/transferring firearms to others…. [F]ederal licensure and record keeping requirements do not affect an individual's rights to possess firearms…. [T]hese requirements affect only the seller. As such, Defendants have failed to persuade this Court that these commercial licensure and recordkeeping requirements implicate the Second Amendment.".

Or as the dissent puts it simply, "the Second Amendment … doesn't mention sellers," so "I do not think that the sellers of guns are covered.".

According to recent reports, by that logic, the First Amendment doesn't mention sellers, so presumably booksellers aren't covered by the First Amendment, either. But that can't be right.

It has been revealed that constitutional rights are constitutional rights, regardless of whether they're compensated—as I've noted on a number of occasions. And if that's true under the First Amendment, then it should be equally true in Second Amendment challenges to § 922(a) as well….

It has been revealed that our dissenting colleague responds by offering a textual distinction between the First and Second Amendments. At bottom, the dissent theorizes that the "freedom of speech" contemplates sales, whereas "the right of the people to keep and bear Arms" does not. But with respect, I don't see the textual distinction that she sees. The theory is also hard to square with what we saw in Villarreal.….

Judge Oldham, joined by Judge Ho, concurred in the judgment (though presumably they also joined their own unsigned opinion):.

It has been revealed that the first question presented is whether restrictions on the sale of firearms burden the Second Amendment rights of American citizens. They do—in at least two ways. First, such restrictions directly burden the seller's right to keep and bear arms. And second, they burden the prospective buyer's right to keep and bear arms, because the right to keep an item always includes the right to acquire it.

It has been revealed that start with the constitutional text. The Second Amendment does not just prohibit the government from denying the right to keep and bear arms. Instead, it claims that the right cannot be "infringed." And at the Founding, "infringe" meant "violate," "destroy," or "hinder." Thus, the government cannot hinder the people's rights to keep and bear arms.

According to recent reports, restrictions on sale hinder both the seller's and buyer's right to keep and bear arms. Start with the seller's right to possess firearms. The Second Amendment guarantees the right to keep guns for personal use, and the seller is an individual who can lawfully possess guns. And it's hornbook property law that the right to possess an article "includes the right to acquire, use, and dispose of it." So the right to keep a gun must include the right to dispose of that gun as the owner sees fit. This is not an independent "right to sell." Rather, my point is that governmental interference with the right to sell a firearm is itself a burden on the seller's existing property right in that firearm. It hinders and hence infringes the seller's rights.

According to recent reports, the same logic applies to the buyer. The buyer's ability to keep and bear arms is certainly "infringed" by regulations that hinder the purchase of arms. After all, the Supreme Court has explained that inherent in "property" is the "right to acquire, use, and dispose of it." In other words, a restriction on the sale of weapons obviously impacts the buyer's constitutional rights to acquire weapons. As one scholar has explained it:.

Industry observers note that because one cannot 'keep' or 'bear' something without acquiring it, the act of acquiring arms must be included in the Second Amendment's 'right to keep and bear arms.' This is true for the same reason that the right to speak would be largely ineffective if it did not include the right to engage in financial transactions that are the incidents of its exercise. For there comes a point at which the regulation of action intimately and unavoidably connected with a right is a regulation of the right itself.

Joseph G.S. Greenlee, The American Tradition of Self-Made Arms, 54 St. Mary's L.J. 35 (2023).

In a recent development, this principle is not limited to the Second Amendment context. For example, consider the neighboring First Amendment. The Free Speech Clause "afford[s] the public access to discussion, debate, and the dissemination of information and ideas"—and thus clearly protects the right to sell and distribute speech, including speech written or produced by others. And it protects the recipient's right to receive information and ideas. Willis v. Town of Marshall (9th Cir. 2002) (Kozinski, J., concurring) ("[T]he right to hear and the right to speak are flip sides of the same coin."). Without a right to provide speech, there is no right to receive information and ideas.

Likewise, consider the Free Exercise Clause. "[T]he text of the Free Exercise Clause gives a specific group of people (those who wish to engage in the 'exercise of religion') the right to do so without hindrance." It is axiomatic that the right to free exercise of religion includes the right to practice it with others in, for example, houses of worship. Shutting down houses of worship is an obvious First Amendment violation for many reasons—not the least of which is that it prevents the faithful from communing with each other and with church leaders who provide teaching, holy sacraments, and other sacred traditions. Thus, the right to exercise religion includes a First Amendment freedom to participate in religious services with—and provide religious services to—others.

These examples demonstrate clear principles. A right to property, free speech, corporate worship, and firearms includes the right to provide these things. And to acquire them….

Industry observers note that judge Oldham also discussed the proper scope of a Fifth Circuit decision, U.S. v. Peterson (5th Cir. 2025) and concludes that it (1) "was wrong and should be overturned" and in any event (2) doesn't apply here; for more on that, read the full opinion.

Judge Catharina Haynes dissented:.

I do not think that the sellers of guns are covered by the Second Amendment (which doesn't mention sellers) …. {Second Amendment is quite different from the First Amendment mentioned in the concurrence. The First Amendment states "freedom of speech" and lists people in general which is quite large whereas the Second Amendment says "the right of people to keep and bear Arms" not mentioning selling Arms or all situations.}.

In a recent development, [But] I am respectful of the majority opinion on that given our prior cases and what the government noted. So, even assuming arguendo the sellers are covered, I see nothing in this case that highlights that the rules for the sellers in this context are inappropriate and, therefore, unconstitutional. Also, to me, since Deare did not properly challenge the relevant rules to show that they are abusive, I do not see a need to remand on that. To me, the relevant rules as to him are sufficient and proper, so I would simply affirm.

I appreciate Judge Ho's and Judge Oldham's arguments that the right to keep and bear arms must include the right to acquire them, which in turn means that restrictions on sales must be evaluated to make sure they don't improperly burden the rights of would-be buyers. By way of analogy, the Court continues to recognize a right to use contraceptives (see Griswold v. Connecticut). Surely that must mean that a ban on selling contraceptives would unconstitutionally burden the would-be buyers' rights, and even less comprehensive restrictions on selling them might likewise be seen as too burdensome.

It has been revealed that but I'm skeptical of the argument that the Second Amendment secures a right of sellers independent of the right of buyers. A bookseller may be mentioned to be engaged in "speech" in the sense that conveying ideas to readers is a form of speech (including when one conveys them in exchange for money). A gun seller, on the other hand, isn't actually "keeping" a gun or "bearing" it. And though property rights do generally include the right to convey, including by sale, I don't think the Second Amendment should be seen as constitutionalizing that.

By way of analogy, the law bans transferring guns to felons. That, the Court has said, is presumptively constitutional, because felons don't have the right to possess guns (focusing on the rights of the would-be gun possessor). But I don't think it follows that the law even implicates the right of gun sellers. When the law bans me from selling a gun to a felon, it isn't affecting my own ability to keep or bear the gun at all.

It has been revealed that and this distinction between (1) the Second Amendment protecting gun sales as facilitative of the buyer's ability to have a gun, and (2) the Second Amendment gun sales as protecting the seller's own Second Amendment rights, may be practically significant. Under theory 1, there would likely be more room for regulation of sellers, since restrictions that only very modestly affect the buyer's ability to buy guns might then be viewed as presumptively constitutional. (That's consistent with D.C. v. Heller's statement that "nothing in our opinion should be taken to cast doubt on … laws imposing conditions and qualifications on the commercial sale of arms"). Under theory 2, there would be less room for regulation of sellers, since the sellers' own rights would be at stake as well.

Again, that's also how the distinction might play out as to the right to use contraceptives, and how it played out as to abortion in the pre-Dobbs Roe/Casey era. For instance, the right to abortion was consistent with licensure requirements for people or organizations that perform abortions, so long as this didn't unduly interfere with women's ability to get abortions. Likewise, it seems to me, the Second Amendment right to keep and bear arms is consistent with licensure requirements for gun sellers, so long as it doesn't unduly interfere with people's ability to get guns that they can then keep and bear.

The economy is growing strongly, so why is nobody hiring?

The latest data show growth hit 3.4% in the third quarter of this year, faster than expected. Yet during that same quarter, the economy only added about 50,000 jobs per month—basically flat in an economy of 330 million people.

Betting markets are forecasting a small uptick: 70,000 last month, less than population growth, in a supposedly sizzling economy. The puzzle is low hiring combined with unemployment at only 4.2%, where it's been for pretty much a year and a half, while jobless claims are actually near historic lows.

It has been revealed that in other words, companies aren't firing workers; they're just not hiring fresh ones. That’s odd since booming GDP usually spawns jobs like mushrooms after rain. The reason could be artificial intelligence—“super intelligence,” if you didn't get the memo.

It has been revealed that the theory is that AI isn't crushing jobs by the millions, but it’s encouraging companies to do more with the people they've got because the technology is providing massive productivity gains. That means firms are delaying latest hires.

Recent findings suggest that the first casualties are recent college grads, especially those destined for America's cubicle farms. An August Stanford study found that employment among 22- to-25-year-olds in AI-exposed occupations was almost 20% below low-exposed jobs, with that gap up by one-third in the last year.

>>> What AI Means for the Future of Work.

Meanwhile, experienced workers have no gap—just the fresh hires. So it’s junior programmers, administrative assistants, entry-level analysts and the army of recent graduates whose job was to rearrange PowerPoint to entertain middle managers.

Sources indicate that this is creating an interesting labor market where experienced workers are valuable because they're actually more efficient with AI, since it’s a force multiplier. But for those with no industry expertise, it’s multiplying zero, which means nothing.

That means upcoming graduates can't get their initial workplace experience because AI replaced them before they even highlighted up. So, AI's not taking all the jobs, but it is taking the first rung of the career ladder in certain sectors.

We've seen this movie before. In 1900, half of American workers were employed in agriculture. Along came tractors and combines, and today it's less than 2%. Yet America didn't end up with 38% unemployment back then because the newly introduced machines freed agriculture workers to make cars and airplanes, and eventually to write software, be personal trainers and fill other jobs.

According to recent reports, it was the same story when computers eliminated typists, bookkeepers and clerks. Millions of jobs were simultaneously created in software, telecommunications, online commerce and fulfillment centers.

Industry observers note that technology doesn't simply eliminate work. Rather, it makes workers more productive, lowers costs, increases purchasing power—so customers buy more stuff—and opens opportunities that didn't exist. The entire Keynesian notion of aggregate demand is a fallacy because humans have unlimited wants.

>>> The Tale of the Disappearing Jobs Numbers.

There will always be demand for more products and services, including things that haven’t been invented yet. The catch is that those new jobs don't appear automatically. Entrepreneurs have to create them, which is why Steve Jobs was such a visionary for inventing the smartphone.

According to recent reports, unfortunately, the creation of latest enterprises is where governments enter the story. Starting a business or hiring your first employee can mean licenses, zoning, permits, tax registrations, insurance mandates, payroll compliance, labor-law restrictions and more. It’s an obstacle course trying to crush the next wave of jobs.

Industry observers note that these matter most to small companies, precisely from where the next generation of jobs should come. New business establishments already create roughly 4 million jobs a year. But imagine how much faster that’d be if starting a business or hiring an employee was like ordering a T-shirt on Amazon.

The solution isn't to ban technology any more than it was to ban tractors or electricity. It's to unleash tomorrow's entrepreneurs.

Slash occupational licensing, payroll taxes, employment-law complexity, and strip away unnecessary permits and zoning. Make it easy to start a business, experiment and hire the first employee.

According to recent reports, technology has been eliminating jobs for thousands of years. In fact, that's how we became rich—the industrial revolution wiping out farm laborers. But what we didn't have in 1840 was an empire of taxes and regulations roadblocking millions of upcoming jobs.

If that doesn't change, this time will, in fact, be different.

It has been revealed that every day, the federal government spends nearly $3 billion on interest on its debt. That’s almost $120 million per hour—and it only covers the cost of past borrowing.

When the Federal Reserve held interest rates steady on Oct. 28, many in Washington and across the country were hoping for a cut, but the Federal Open Market Committee kept its target range for the federal funds rate at 3.75% to 4.00%.

Industry observers note that the Fed’s decision increases borrowing costs for families and businesses, weighing on everything from mortgages to business investment. There’s also an uncomfortable consequence for Washington: It makes financing an already enormous federal debt even more expensive.

Industry observers note that the U.S. national debt now exceeds $40 trillion, roughly 126% of GDP, and continues to climb. The last time the federal government recorded a budget surplus was in 2001 when the debt was only $5 trillion. America’s national debt has skyrocketed eightfold in a quarter century, with no signs of slowing down.

Recent findings suggest that as the size of the debt grows, the cost of carrying it also increases. But that’s not an argument for easier monetary policy. It’s an argument for responsible fiscal policy.

>>> No, Mamdani, Socialism Does Not Increase Affordability.

Last year, the U.S. collected $5.5 trillion in revenues and spent $7.5 trillion in outlays, running a $2 trillion deficit. Interest on the $40 trillion debt accounted for nearly $1.3 trillion of that spending. To finance deficits, the government borrows by issuing securities, primarily Treasury bills, notes, and bonds.

Sources indicate that when investors expect persistently higher inflation, they demand higher yields to compensate for the expected erosion of purchasing power. That pushes Treasury yields higher, making upcoming federal borrowing more expensive.

With Washington already carrying $40 trillion in debt and persistently running large deficits, higher borrowing costs increase the government’s interest burden.

The result is a doom loop cycle: substantial debt leads to higher interest costs, wider deficits, more borrowing, and still more debt.

This is why the Federal Reserve acts, and not in the way Washington may prefer.

Sources indicate that the Fed doesn’t exist to keep the government’s borrowing costs low. Its “dual mandate” is to maximize total employment and maintain price stability. The Bureau of Economic Analysis estimated August 2026 inflation at 3.4%, still above the 2% stated target. This supports the Fed’s continued focus on curbing inflation and, more importantly, inflationary expectations.

Industry observers note that demanding the Fed suppress interest rates to make borrowing cheaper merely attacks the symptom, not the disease. Though lower rates can address affordability concerns and ease pressure on federal deficits, restoring price stability will require higher interest rates for potentially longer periods once households and investors expect higher inflation.

For long-term price stability, it was crucial that the Fed send the signal that it remains committed to protecting the purchasing power of the dollar, even when doing so comes at a short-term cost—namely interest payments.

Sources indicate that interest on the national debt is expected to reach $2.1 trillion by fiscal 2036, making it the third-largest single-line item on the budget and nearly 20% of federal spending. The Congressional Budget Office projects annual federal deficits will rise from $1.9 trillion to $3.1 trillion in the next decade, partially driven by rising interest costs. The CBO also estimates that if interest rates were 1.5% above expectations, cumulative deficits would increase by $6.0 trillion, even if Congress doesn’t enact additional spending.

>>> How to Thaw the Frozen Housing Market.

Sources indicate that left unchecked, rising rates and debt-service costs create an increasingly vicious fiscal cycle: more revenue goes toward servicing yesterday’s borrowing, leaving less room for today’s priorities and forcing Washington to borrow more. Eventually, policymakers face increasingly painful choices over taxes, spending, and entitlement reform.

It has been revealed that the Federal Reserve didn’t create Washington’s $40 trillion debt. Congress and leaders of both parties did. The Fed shouldn’t feel pressured to erase the consequences of decades of deficit spending by keeping interest rates artificially low. That responsibility falls on Congress.

Lawmakers must put the federal budget on a sustainable long-term path toward balance. Ensuring generated revenues cover all non-interest spending, known as a “primary balance,” can be achieved by voting in representatives who support fiscal responsibility.

Waste and fraud should be rooted out wherever they exist, but those savings cannot substitute for confronting the structural drivers of federal spending. The CBO projects that government spending on Social Security and Medicare, along with interest payments, will grow faster than the economy over the coming decade. Any serious fiscal proposal must acknowledge that.

For decades, Democrats and Republicans seemingly agreed with unlimited spending and only disagreed over what it should be spent on. The Federal Reserve is not responsible for today’s fiscal problem or the solution. The Fed’s job is to protect the value of the dollar, not the value of Washington’s borrowing habit.

In a recent development, the Fed got it right. Now Washington needs to do the same.

The California Supreme Court has once again mistaken judicial invention for constitutional interpretation. In April, the court held that, except in capital cases, the California Constitution guarantees criminal defendants a right to pretrial release on bail—and requires trial judges to set bail at an amount that is “reasonably attainable” by the accused.[REF] That holding is as novel as it is alarming. It elevates a judge-made entitlement over the text, history, and structure of the state constitution; discounts the grave risks that some defendants pose to victims and the public; and disregards the repeated, unmistakable commands of the California electorate.Californians have confronted this pattern before. Again and again, the state’s high court has purported to discover sweeping rights for criminals in the California Constitution that the document’s text does not fairly support—only to have the people restore constitutional order at the ballot box. Propositions 4, 8, 9, and 189 were not isolated political reactions. Each was a referendum passed in response to radical decisions that placed the interests of criminals above the rights of victims, the protection of the public, and the common-sense judgments of the citizenry. Each reflected the sovereign authority of the people to correct a court that had strayed from the constitution it was charged with interpreting.The latest bail decision repeats that error in particularly stark form. During the past 44 years, California voters have amended their constitution not once but twice, both to make clear that trial judges may deny bail to a person charged with a felony and to establish a Victims’ Bill of Rights—including mandatory detention for violent felons who pose a threat to others.[REF] Those amendments cannot be reconciled with the court’s upcoming affordable bail standard. The court’s contrary conclusion does not merely misread the charter; it diminishes the constitutional choices the people themselves have made.This Legal Memorandum proceeds in three parts. Part I traces the California Supreme Court’s recurring practice of constitutional innovation and the electorate’s repeated use of the initiative and referendum process to reject it, with particular attention to Propositions 4, 8, 9, and 189. Part II examines the text, history, and purpose of California’s bail provisions and Victims’ Bill of Rights, showing how those provisions preserve judicial authority to deny bail when necessary to protect victims and public safety. Part III analyzes the court’s April decision, identifies its doctrinal and practical defects, and explains why its “reasonably attainable” standard cannot be squared with the constitution as amended by the people.The court’s latest holding is contrary to the text of California’s constitution, contrary to its history, and contrary to the settled will of the people. It should not be permitted to stand. The people of California—or, where constitutionally sufficient, their elected representatives—should correct the court once again and reaffirm a basic principle of ordered liberty: The criminal justice system exists not only to protect the rights of the accused, but also to vindicate the rights of victims, punish criminals, and safeguard the public.Part I: Judicial Innovation v. the ElectorateCalifornia’s original constitution of 1849 provided that “all persons shall be bailable, by sufficient sureties; unless for capital offences, when the proof is evident or the presumption great.”[REF] Another provision stated that “excessive bail shall not be required, nor excessive fines imposed, nor shall cruel or unusual punishments be inflicted, nor shall witnesses be unreasonably detained.”[REF] In 1879, those two provisions were consolidated into Article I, Section 6 of the Constitution of 1879. That remained the case for almost 100 years.In 1973, the California Supreme Court held in In re Underwood that the right to pretrial release was guaranteed for all defendants.[REF] Displeased with the court’s ruling, voters passed Proposition 7 in 1974, relocated the bail provisions to Section 12, and gave trial judges the discretion to release defendants on their own recognizance.[REF]In 1977, Governor Jerry Brown appointed Rose Bird as Chief Justice of the California Supreme Court. Bird was divisive and controversial in part because of her consistent votes against capital convictions[REF] and a dissent she wrote opposing the inclusion of Proposition 8—the Victim’s Bill of Rights—on the ballot in 1982.[REF] She was eventually removed from office in 1986 by the voters.By 1982, having had enough of rogue judges and violent criminals, California voters passed two propositions to amend the constitution to shorten the leash on judges and bolster victims’ rights. The first was Proposition 4, a constitutional amendment that allowed courts to deny bail in felony cases under two additional circumstances. As amended, Section 12 stated:A person shall be released on bail by sufficient sureties, except for: (a) Felony offenses involving acts of violence against another person when the facts are evident or the presumption great and the court finds based upon clear and convincing evidence that there is a substantial likelihood the person’s release would result in great bodily harm to others or; (b) Felony offenses when the facts are evident or the presumption great and the court finds based on clear and convincing evidence that the person has threatened another person with great bodily harm and that there is a substantial likelihood that the person would carry out the threat if released.[REF]The voters passed Proposition 4 by an overwhelming vote of 82.5 percent to 15.1 percent to prevent both the legislature and judges from changing the requirements that governed bail without the people’s consent.[REF]The second was Proposition 8, which amended the state constitution by including a victim’s bill of rights and restricting the rights of convicts.[REF] Adopted by a vote of 56 percent to 43 percent, Proposition 8 repealed Section 12 of Article I and added Section 28, which included the following prefatory language: “The People of the State of California find and declare that the enactment of comprehensive provisions and laws ensuring a bill of rights for victims of crime, including safeguards in the crime justice system to fully protect those rights, is a matter of grave statewide concern.”[REF] Section 28(e), entitled “Public Safety Bail,” stated in part:A person may be released on bail by sufficient sureties, except for capital crimes when the facts are evident or the presumption great…. In setting, reducing or denying bail, the judge or magistrate shall take into consideration the protection of the public, the seriousness of the offense charged, the previous criminal record of the defendant, and the probability of his or her appearing at the trial or hearing of the case. Public safety shall be the primary consideration.[REF]Taken together, Propositions 4 and 8 sent a loud and clear message that the citizens of California were fed up with judges releasing violent felons, that mandatory release on bail was a bridge too far, that victims mattered, and that public safety—not defendant’s “rights”—was the “primary consideration” that judges must take into account when setting bail.In 1994, the voters passed Proposition 189, which, among other things, amended Article I, Section 12 by adding “felony sexual assault offenses on another person” to subsection (b).[REF] A year later, in In re York, a case dealing with whether a court or magistrate may condition release from custody on a defendant’s own recognizance, the California Supreme Court noted in a footnote that the bail provision language in Proposition 4 appeared to conflict with the language in Proposition 8 (“shall” in Proposition 4 vs. “may” in Proposition 8) and that, because Proposition 4 received more votes, its bail and own recognizance provisions were “deemed to prevail over those set forth in Proposition 8.”[REF] In other words, trial judges “shall” (i.e., must) release defendants on bail unless it is a capital case or one of the felony exceptions enumerated in subsections (b) or (c). Remarkably, the court did not cite any statute or state constitutional provision authorizing it to erase the will of the voters and nullify Proposition 8 because Proposition 4 received more votes.In 2006, the California Supreme Court held in People v. Standish that, because the bail provisions of Propositions 4 and 8 were “directly at odds,” Section 28(e) of Proposition 8 “never took effect.”[REF] So much for the 2,826,081 Californians who voted for Proposition 8.Angered by crime rates and a state Supreme Court that did not put victims first, California voters passed Proposition 9, the “Victim’s Bill of Rights Act of 2008,” called Marsy’s Law.[REF] Proposition 9 specified that the law, named for Marsy Nicholas, who was murdered by her ex-boyfriend in 1983, was “needed to remedy a justice system that fails to fully recognize and adequately enforce rights of victims of crime.”[REF] In the “Findings and Declarations” section, Marsy’s Law says that “[t]he People of the State of California find that the ‘broad reform’ of the criminal justice system intended to grant these basic rights mandated in the Victims’ Bill of Rights initiative measure passed by the electorate as Proposition 8 in 1982 has not occurred as envisioned by the people,” a not-so-subtle swipe at the California Supreme Court and its abandonment of Proposition 8.[REF]Marsy’s Law amended Section 28 of Article I of the state’s constitution by enumerating victims’ rights “in order to protect the legitimate rights of victims of crime.”[REF] Key among those rights were (1) the right to “have the safety of the victim and the victim’s family considered in fixing the amount of bail and release conditions for the defendant” under Section 28(b)(3) and (2) the right to public safety bail: “A person may be released on bail by sufficient sureties, except for capital crime when the facts are evident…. [I]n setting, reducing or denying bail, the judge or magistrate shall take into consideration the protection of the public, the safety of the victim, the seriousness of the offense charged…. [P]ublic safety and the safety of the victim shall be the primary considerations” under Section 28(f)(3).[REF]Notice how California voters again adopted language to reject the California Supreme Court, this time to rebut the court’s creative erasure of the bail provisions of Proposition 8. By using “may” instead of “shall,” the people made clear both that judges do indeed have the discretion to deny bail and that the safety of the victim must be the primary consideration.Part II: Cash Bail and Victims’ RightsCash bail rests on a straightforward proposition: Pretrial liberty and accountability need not be opposing principles. By placing a financial stake behind a defendant’s promise to return to court, bail supplies a concrete incentive to appear while permitting release pending adjudication—not punishment before conviction. From the perspective of the California District Attorneys Association (CDAA) and other prosecutor associations across the country, traditional cash bail remains an important component of a pretrial system charged with protecting the public and securing defendants’ appearance. Bail schedules give that system a practical framework: Predetermined, offense-based amounts provide a consistent starting point, make release requirements more predictable, and can allow eligible defendants to obtain release without waiting for an initial court appearance.Properly understood, however, a schedule is a starting point, not a substitute for judicial judgment. Neither money nor a printed chart guarantees public safety or attendance; individualized review must account for the defendant’s circumstances and ability to pay, available nonfinancial alternatives, and applicable constitutional protections. The sound argument for bail schedules is therefore not that they eliminate discretion, but that they discipline its exercise, providing an orderly framework within which courts can reconcile liberty, accountability, and public safety.As a policy matter, the push to end cash bail is not new in our country. In 1961, progressives created the Manhattan Bail Project specifically to eliminate cash bail.[REF] That project eventually grew into the Vera Institute and dozens of other organizations like Vera that are obsessed with ending cash bail. They even came up with spooky-sounding terms like “poverty penalty,” suggesting that the only reason a person remained in jail pending trial was his or her inability to post bond, ignoring the facts of the crime alleged or history of failures to appear in court or long criminal records—the Achilles’ heels of the movement. In 2017, former career public defender Robin Steinberg founded the Bail Project, an organization the provides free bail assistance to those who cannot afford to post bail, in California.[REF]In 2018, the California Senate passed S.B. 10, a law designed to eliminate cash bail in the state and replace it with mandatory risk assessments for detained suspects awaiting trial.[REF] After the governor signed the bill, a unique mix of stakeholders banded together to repeal the legislation by referendum during the November 2020 election. Supporters of the “no” vote to repeal the controversial legislation included, in addition to the California Republican Party, the American Civil Liberties Union (ACLU) of Southern California, California Black Chamber of Commerce, California NAACP, and Crime Victims United of California, among other groups. The “yes” vote effort was backed by the California Democratic Party and included financial support from Patty Quillin ($1 million, the wife of Netflix CEO Reed Hastings; Steve and Connie Ballmer of Microsoft ($6 million total); and Tom Steyer, founder of Farallon Capital hedge fund and the NextGen Climate Action Committee ($500,000).[REF] California Proposition 25 repealed S.B. 10 by a margin of 56.41 percent to 43.59 percent and effectively restored cash bail.[REF]That same year, George Gascon was elected Los Angeles County District Attorney, in large part because of an infusion of $2.5 million from George Soros, who gave the money to the California Justice & Safety PAC, which supported Gascon’s campaign.[REF] Upon election, Gascon set up a transition team populated with 38 anti–law-and-order activists and zealots tasked with implementing his progressive (including anti–cash bail) agenda.[REF] This was significant because the Los Angeles County District Attorney’s Office is the largest DA’s office in the country, with upwards of 900-plus prosecutors spread across the massive county. Since one of the hallmarks of the Soros rogue prosecutor movement was to eliminate cash bail, Gascon’s “bail committee” was headed by Robin Steinberg and Dolores Caneles, Community Outreach Director for the Bail Project.[REF]Moments after Gascon was sworn into office, he issued a blizzard of policy directives. Special Directive 20-06, concerning “Pretrial Release Policy,” claimed that “unaffordable cash bail” creates “a two-tiered system of justice,” leads to “unnecessary incarceration,” and “eviscerates the bedrock of our democracy and undermines our principles of justice, fairness and equality under the law.”[REF] Even though Proposition 25 had just failed, the directive stated the D.A.’s Office “will not wait for statewide reform before imposing meaningful changes in the use of cash bail.”[REF] In what has become a mantra for the anti-bail cabal, the directive blurted out that “freedom should be free.”[REF]The directive does not mention that certain criminals, especially career felons, pose a significant risk of danger to the community and that cash bail is a tool that works to ensure their appearance at future court dates. Nor does the directive mention the law (such as Marsy’s Law), victims’ rights in the California Constitution, or the fact that public safety is and should be the “primary consideration” when setting the appropriate amount of bail.Gascon’s diktat prohibited his prosecutors from taking into consideration an accused’s criminal history, requesting cash bail for any misdemeanor, and relying solely on scored risk assessment tools for detention.[REF] In a move that likely upset career prosecutors in his office, Gascon’s directive prohibited them from opposing defense motions to remove or modify conditions of release, defense requests to waive client appearances at “non-essential” court proceedings, or defense requests seeking relief from bench warrants for defendants who fail to appear.[REF] In other words, Gascon prevented his prosecutors from being prosecutors.Other Soros-funded or Soros-inspired California prosecutors such as Chesa Boudin (San Francisco), Pamela Price (Alameda), and Diana Becton (Contra Costa) instituted similar anti-cash bail policies that predictably resulted in rising crime rates in their counties.[REF]Part III: Humphrey and KowalczykTwo years before Proposition 25 repealed S.B. 10 but after S.B. 10 was the law in California, the Court of Appeals for the First District of California held in In Re Kenneth Humphrey that a trial judge (1) failed to make findings and inquiries regarding the financial ability of the defendant to post bail; (2) failed to consider whether less restrictive conditions of release were available; and (3) set bail based solely on the bail schedule rather than on an individualized inquiry.[REF] As a result, the appeals court reversed and remanded the case to the trial court. The trial court conducted a new bail hearing and ordered Humphrey released on various non-financial conditions.The issue was resolved, and there was no live case or controversy, but that did not stop the California Supreme Court from wading into the issue. Typically, the top appellate court in a state takes cases only where there is a live case or controversy. But not in California, where its Supreme Court injected itself into the bail debate by granting review on its own motion in the Humphrey case. In a 2021 opinion, the court noted that it granted review “to address the constitutionality of money bail as right now used in California as well as the proper role of public and victim safety in making bail determinations.”[REF]Despite the fact that Humphrey had won his case and obtained the relief he sought, the court held that “where a financial condition is nonetheless necessary, the court must consider the arrestee’s ability to pay the state amount of bail—and may not effectively detain the arrestee solely because the arrestee lacked the resources to post bail.”[REF] The court handed down its decision on March 21, 2021—four months after November 3, 2020, when the voters had soundly rejected Proposition 25 and its idea of eliminating cash bail and replacing it with a scheme based on risk assessment—and did not even mention the results of Proposition 25 in its opinion.The court noted that in “unusual circumstances” when the “need to protect community safety may conflict with the arrestee’s fundamental right to pretrial liberty…[ to detain an arrestee] a court must find by clear and convincing evidence that no condition short of detention could suffice and then ensure [that] the detention otherwise complies with statutory constitutional requirements.”[REF] If Justice Antonin Scalia had been on the Humphrey court, he would have ridiculed the majority’s “interpretive jiggery-pokery.”[REF]Courts have no business opining on hypothetical concerns or issuing policy statements under the fig leaf of a judicial opinion. Our Founders realized this and embedded limitations on the jurisdiction of United States federal courts in Article III, Section 2, Clause 1 of the U.S. Constitution. As the Supreme Court noted in Flast v. Cohen, the judicial power of the federal courts “is constitutionally restricted to ‘cases’ and ‘controversies.’”[REF] Those two words “have an iceberg quality, containing beneath their surface simplicity submerged complexities which go to the very heart of our constitutional form of government.”[REF] Those two words “limit the business of federal courts to questions presented in an adversary context and in a form historically viewed as capable of resolution through the judicial process.”[REF]Similar to the federal Constitution, the California Constitution divides the power of the government among the legislative, executive, and judicial branches, but it does not contain a case-or-controversy clause. Under Article VI, Section 12(a), the state’s Supreme Court “may, before decision, transfer to itself a cause in a court of appeal.”[REF] Under Subsection (b), however, the “Supreme Court may review the decision of a court of appeal in any cause.”[REF] The California Supreme Court has interpreted this clause as allowing it to issue advisory opinions, and the “cause” it took up here was obvious: Draft an opinion that discovers a constitutional right to affordable bail and enshrine that right across the state despite the will of the people as recently affirmed by the result of Proposition 25. The court did not cite Section 12 as a justification to render an advisory opinion.Amicus briefs in support of Humphrey included Chesa Boudin, a San Francisco Deputy Public Defender, various ACLU offices across California, the California Public Defenders Association, and the American Bar Association.[REF] Amicus briefs supporting the People of California included elected district attorneys George Gascon, Summer Stephan, Michael Ramos, and (at least at first) Xavier Becerra, the state’s Attorney General.[REF]The unanimous decision reads like a policy paper from the Bail Project. The decision notes that an “accused may be impaired to some extent in preparing a defense” and that “studies suggest that pretrial detention heightens the risk of losing a job,” referencing two slanted law review articles critical of pretrial detention, one of which was published by Harvard Law School’s Criminal Justice Program (CJP).[REF]The two issues not resolved in Humphrey were (1) whether Section 12 of the state constitution “can or should be” reconciled with the public safety bail provision of Marsy’s Law in Section 28(f)(3) and (2) whether it is constitutionally permissible for a trial court to set bail above a defendant’s ability to pay.The court did not note that the lead author of the Harvard paper was Elana Fogel of the ACLU’s Initiative to Combat Mass Incarceration[REF] or that one of the two faculty co-directors of the CJP was Professor Carol Steiker, a zealous anti–death penalty advocate.[REF] Nor did the court mention the fact that among other people who provided “generous insights and feedback” to the paper were none other than Patrisse Cullors, a radical Marxist, avowed prison abolitionist, and co-founder of Black Lives Matter, and Alec Karakatsanis, a public defender and fellow traveler on the abolish-prisons train.[REF]To justify its opinion, the court wrote that “principles of equal protection and substantive due process likewise converge in the money bail context. The accused retains the fundamental constitutional right to liberty,” citing the Supreme Court’s opinion in United States v. Salerno.[REF] The problem for the court is that Salerno did not say that. In fact, Salerno held (1) that the federal Bail Reform Act’s authorization of pretrial detention on the basis of future dangerousness constituted a permissible regulation that did not violate substantive due process and was not impermissible punishment before trial and (2) that the Due Process Clause did not categorically prohibit pretrial detention imposed as a regulatory measure on the ground of community danger.[REF] The page in Salerno that the California Supreme Court referenced in its opinion for the proposition that an accused “retains the fundamental right to liberty” was ripped out of context.In analyzing the Bail Reform Act’s procedures, the U.S. Supreme Court contrasted the “government’s interest in preventing crime,” which it described as “both legitimate and compelling,” with the “other side of the scale…the individual’s strong interest in liberty.”[REF] The Court noted the “importance and fundamental nature of this right” but then added that, “as our cases hold, this right may, in circumstances where the government’s interest is sufficiently weighty, be subordinated to the greater needs of society.”[REF] Nevertheless, the California Supreme Court held in Humphrey that pretrial detention based solely on an accused’s financial condition violates state and federal equal protection and due process principles.[REF]Those cases set the stage for the latest outrage from the California Supreme Court. In In re Kowalczyk, the court addressed two important questions left unresolved by In re Humphrey: whether Article I, Section 12, or Article I, Section 28(f)(3) of the California Constitution controls the denial of bail in noncapital cases and whether a trial court may set monetary bail above a defendant’s ability to pay. The case arose after Gerald Kowalczyk used several lost credit cards at a fast-food restaurant and was charged with identity theft and related offenses. The allegations themselves were comparatively modest, but Kowalczyk’s record was anything but modest: He had accumulated 64 prior convictions, had failed to comply with supervision while previously released on his own recognizance, and had convictions in multiple counties and states.The trial court first set bail at $75,000 and later denied bail altogether, citing Kowalczyk’s extensive criminal history, his poor record of compliance, and the substantial risk that he would not appear for future proceedings. While Kowalczyk’s habeas petition was pending, he accepted a plea agreement, received credit for time served, and was released.The Court of Appeal initially dismissed the petition as moot, but the California Supreme Court transferred the matter back with instructions to decide the constitutional questions. The case thus became the vehicle for resolving a conflict among the Courts of Appeal over the meaning of California’s competing bail provisions and the reach of Humphrey.The dispute centered on two commands adopted at different times: Section 12’s direction that a person “shall be released on bail,” subject to enumerated exceptions for specified violent or threatening felonies, and Marsy’s Law’s later declaration in Section 28(f)(3) that a person “may be released on bail” and that public safety and victim safety “shall be the primary considerations” when bail is set, reduced, or denied.The court held that the two provisions could be “harmonized,” but only by treating Section 12 as the controlling limitation on judicial authority. In the court’s view, Section 12 supplies the exclusive categories in which bail may be denied in a noncapital case: certain violent felonies, felony sexual assaults, and other felonies involving threats of great bodily harm, coupled with the constitutionally required findings.Section 28(f)(3), the court reasoned, does not enlarge those categories. Instead, its use of the word “may” describes only the possibility that a defendant may or may not be released, while its references to public safety, victim safety, and “denying bail” operate only within Section 12’s preexisting framework. Relying on the presumption against implied repeal, the court concluded that Marsy’s Law neither displaced Section 12 nor gave judges broader authority to detain dangerous defendants charged with offenses outside Section 12’s enumerated exceptions.On the second question, the court held that when preventive detention is unavailable under Section 12, bail generally must be set at an amount reasonably attainable by the particular defendant. A court must first consider whether nonfinancial conditions—such as supervision, monitoring, or required check-ins—can reasonably protect the public, safeguard the victim, and assure the defendant’s appearance. If monetary bail is necessary, the judge must conduct an individualized assessment that includes the seriousness of the offense, the defendant’s criminal record, compliance history, flight risk, danger to others, financial resources, and the availability of less restrictive alternatives. The amount need not be convenient or easily affordable, and a defendant must substantiate a claimed inability to pay. But a judge may not deliberately set an insurmountable figure as an end run around Section 12’s limits on detention.Although its conclusion may be dressed in the familiar robes of harmonization, the court once again managed to find a creative way to write around what the people enacted. Marsy’s Law did not say that public safety and victim safety should merely be considered after judges had exhausted the narrow detention categories contained in Section 12. It declared that a person “may” be released on bail; expressly governed the “setting, reducing, or denying” of bail; and commanded that public safety and victim safety “shall be the primary considerations.” Those words were adopted against a well-developed constitutional history in which the difference between “shall” and “may” had already carried unmistakable significance. Rather than give the voters’ chosen language its ordinary force, the court converted “may” into a vague statement of abstract possibility and reduced the public-safety mandate to a procedural appendage. That is not faithful harmonization. It is judicial revision.The court’s reliance on the presumption against implied repeal also obscures the central issue. No one needed to prove that Marsy’s Law silently erased every word of Section 12. The task was to give meaningful effect to both provisions, including the later amendment’s explicit reference to denying bail and its elevation of safety above all other considerations.A genuinely harmonious reading would recognize that Section 12 preserves a general right to bail while Section 28(f)(3) grants courts discretion to deny it when compelling public-safety or victim-safety concerns demand that result. Instead, the court treated the older provision as a ceiling on the newer one, leaving the operative language of Marsy’s Law with remarkably little independent work to do. The result is especially difficult to defend in a case involving a defendant with 64 prior convictions, repeated supervision failures, and a demonstrated history spanning multiple jurisdictions—the very sort of record that makes a categorical refusal to recognize broader judicial discretion appear detached from practical reality.Just as troubling is the court’s dismissive treatment of amici curiae on the other side, especially the California District Attorneys Association. The CDAA’s amicus brief made the straightforward textual point that Section 28(f)(3)’s express reference to “denying bail” must do real work; otherwise, the phrase is substantially drained of meaning. The court brushed that argument aside as “unpersuasive,” reasoning that “denying” bail refers only to defendants who are already eligible for detention without bail under Section 12. But that answer assumes the very conclusion the amici challenged.It does not explain why the voters added broader, later language addressing the denial of bail, used “may” instead of “shall,” and made public and victim safety primary if they intended no meaningful expansion of judicial authority.The irony is difficult to miss. The amici’s arguments were grounded in the constitutional text, the history of California’s competing bail provisions, the structure of Marsy’s Law, and the electorate’s unmistakable demand that victims and public safety come first. The California Supreme Court’s contrary logic depends on redefining ordinary words, minimizing later-enacted language, and insulating its preferred result behind an unusually rigid application of the rule against implied repeal.Having disconnected its analysis from the text and from the voters’ evident purpose, the court then pronounced the more natural reading “unpersuasive.” Once again, the people spoke through the initiative process, and once again, the court found a creative way to tell them that the words they enacted do not mean what they plainly say.ConclusionThe California Supreme Court’s outrageous decision in In re Kowalczyk cannot be allowed to stand. Once again, the court has mistaken judicial invention for constitutional interpretation, elevating a newly minted right to “reasonably attainable” bail over the text, structure, and history of California’s constitution—and over the repeated commands of the people themselves. A constitution that makes public safety and victim safety the “primary considerations” cannot fairly be read to require judges to price dangerous or chronically noncompliant defendants out of detention.The response should be immediate and sustained. Congress should hold oversight hearings that examine the consequences of judicially imposed “affordable bail” rules, including their effects on interstate crime, federal–state law-enforcement cooperation, victims, repeat offending, and failures to appear. California’s legislature should likewise conduct public hearings; compel testimony from prosecutors, sheriffs, victims, and pretrial-services officials; and require transparent reporting on rearrests, absconding, supervision failures, and crimes committed by defendants released under the new rule.Most important, Californians should return to the ballot box with a constitutional amendment that leaves no room for further judicial gamesmanship. The amendment should state in plain English that criminal defendants do not have a constitutional right to bail set at an amount they can afford when they are accused of a violent crime, present a serious danger to a victim or the public, pose a substantial flight risk, repeatedly violate release conditions, or have a long criminal record demonstrating chronic recidivism or noncompliance. It should also reaffirm that judges may deny bail in those circumstances and that protection of victims and the public—not a defendant’s financial convenience—remains the primary consideration.Finally, Californians should use every lawful mechanism of judicial accountability that is available to them. If members of the court persist in rewriting voter-enacted constitutional commands, the public should seriously consider recall proceedings against the responsible justices, consistent with California law and with full respect for due process. Judicial independence is not judicial supremacy. The people are sovereign, and their Constitution is binding. No court is entitled to nullify either one by redefining ordinary words so that they mean their opposite.Charles D. Stimson is Acting Director of the Legal Policy Center and Senior Legal Fellow, National Security, at The Heritage Foundation.

In a recent development, the California Supreme Court has once again mistaken judicial invention for constitutional interpretation. In April, the court held that, except in capital cases, the California Constitution guarantees criminal defendants a right to pretrial release on bail—and requires trial judges to set bail at an amount that is “reasonably attainable” by the accused.[REF] That holding is as novel as it is alarming. It elevates a judge-made entitlement over the text, history, and structure of the state constitution; discounts the grave risks that some defendants pose to victims and the public; and disregards the repeated, unmistakable commands of the California electorate.

Each was a referendum passed in response to radical decisions that placed the interests of criminals above the rights of victims, the protection of the public, and the common-sense judgments of the citizenry. Each reflected the sovereign authority of the people to correct a court that had strayed from the constitution it was charged with interpreting.

The latest bail decision repeats that error in particularly stark form. During the past 44 years, California voters have amended their constitution not once but twice, both to make clear that trial judges may deny bail to a person charged with a felony and to establish a Victims’ Bill of Rights—including mandatory detention for violent felons who pose a threat to others.[REF] Those amendments cannot be reconciled with the court’s new affordable bail standard. The court’s contrary conclusion does not merely misread the charter; it diminishes the constitutional choices the people themselves have made.
